To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

diet-induced obese rats had a statistically significant reduction in the number nNOS-immuno labelled cells in the ventral medial hypothalamus (VMH) compared to chow fed animals, that chronic i.p. administration of L- NAME decreased hypothalamic nitro oxide content in both chows and DIO, that energy intake was significantly reduced in DIO over a 16 day period, that energy intake in DIO was more significantly reduced than chow fed animals after i.c.v.

(i) diet-induced obesity is associated with decreased neuronal nitric oxide synthesis in the ventromedia hypothalamus, and that (ii) the sensitivity to inhibition of nitric oxide synthetase is greater in dietary obese rats, suggesting a role of nitric oxide in development of obesity in rats fed palatable diet.
(i) DIO rats have reduced hypothalamic neuronal NO synthase expression; (ii) DIO rats are more sensitive to NOS inhibition; (iii) DIO rats exhibit reduced hypothalamic NO after NOS inhibition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of hypothalamic NO in energy homeostasis, with a particular focus on the ventromedinal hypothalamus, which is a key area for control of feeding.
understanding the role of hypothalamic neuronal NO synthase and its inhibition in the control of bodyweight and energy intake.
the effects of diet on the hypothalamus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of nitric oxide in energy intake and energy balance is complex and that the effect of nitric oxide on energy balance is dependent upon the nutritional state of the animal.
the role of NO in energy homeostasis and obesity is still not completely understood.
the hypothalamic NOS is sensitive to nutritional state and that inhibition of this enzyme may have therapeutic benefits in the treatment of obesity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dietary obese animals are more sensitive to the effect of NO inhibition, and this is likely to be due to the reduced expression of hypothalamic NOS.
NO is an important regulator of energy balance and that changes in NO may contribute to the development of obesity.
the hypothalamic nitroergic system plays a key role in the regulation of body weight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NO may be a key player in the development of obesity in rats fed palatable diets.
the hypothalamic neuronal NO synthase (nNOS)-expressing neurons in the VMH are sensitive to the nutritional state of an animal.
the NOS inhibitor L-NAME reduced bodyweight gain in diet-induced obese animals but not in chows fed animals.
